" Base: {{{1
call tutor#SetupVim()

" Buffer Settings: {{{1
setlocal noreadonly
if !exists('g:tutor_debug') || g:tutor_debug == 0
    setlocal buftype=nofile
    setlocal concealcursor+=inv
    setlocal conceallevel=2
else
    setlocal buftype=
    setlocal concealcursor&
    setlocal conceallevel=0
endif
setlocal noundofile

setlocal keywordprg=:help
setlocal iskeyword=@,-,_

" The user will have to enable the folds himself, but we provide the foldexpr
" function.
setlocal foldmethod=manual
setlocal foldexpr=tutor#TutorFolds()
setlocal foldlevel=4

" Load metadata if it exists: {{{1
if filereadable(expand('%').'.json')
    call tutor#LoadMetadata()
endif

" Mappings: {{{1

call tutor#SetNormalMappings()

" Checks: {{{1

sign define tutorok text=✓ texthl=tutorOK
sign define tutorbad text=✗ texthl=tutorX
======
if exists("b:current_syntax")
    finish
endif

syn include @VIM syntax/vim.vim
unlet b:current_syntax
syn include @TUTORSHELL syntax/sh.vim
unlet b:current_syntax
syn include @VIMNORMAL syntax/vimnormal.vim

syn match tutorLink /\[.\{-}\](.\{-})/ contains=tutorInlineNormal
syn match tutorLinkBands /\[\|\]\|(\|)/ contained containedin=tutorLink,tutorLinkAnchor conceal
syn match tutorLinkAnchor /(.\{-})/ contained containedin=tutorLink conceal
syn match tutorURL /\(https\?\|file\):\/\/[[:graph:]]\+\>\/\?/
syn match tutorEmail /\<[[:graph:]]\+@[[:graph:]]\+\>/
syn match tutorInternalAnchor /\*[[:alnum:]-]\+\*/ contained conceal containedin=tutorSection

syn match tutorSection /^#\{1,6}\s.\+$/ fold contains=tutorInlineNormal
syn match tutorSectionBullet /#/ contained containedin=tutorSection

syn match tutorTOC /\ctable of contents:/

syn match tutorConcealedEscapes /\\[`*!\[\]():$-]\@=/ conceal

syn region tutorEmphasis matchgroup=Delimiter start=/[\*]\@<!\*\*\@!/ end=/[\*]\@<!\*\*\@!/
	    \ concealends contains=tutorInlineCommand,tutorInlineNormal
syn region tutorBold matchgroup=Delimiter start=/\*\{2}/ end=/\*\{2}/
	    \ concealends contains=tutorInlineCommand,tutorInlineNormal

syn keyword tutorMarks TODO NOTE IMPORTANT TIP ATTENTION EXERCISE
syn keyword tutorMarks todo note tip attention exercise
syn keyword tutorMarks Todo Note Tip Excersise

syn region tutorCodeblock matchgroup=Delimiter start=/^\~\{3}.*$/ end=/^\~\{3}/

syn region tutorShell matchgroup=Delimiter start=/^\~\{3} sh\s*$/ end=/^\~\{3}/ keepend contains=@TUTORSHELL concealends
syn match tutorShellPrompt /\(^\s*\)\@<=[$#]/ contained containedin=tutorShell

syn region tutorInlineCode matchgroup=Delimiter start=/\\\@<!`/ end=/\\\@<!\(`{\@!\|`\s\)/ concealends

Very important findings:

1. **Both** editors ship a full `tutor` filetype apparatus (from the "tutor" runtime plugin — markdown-based tutor format, `tutor#ApplyMarks()` with checkmarks, `buftype=nofile`, conceallevel=2, etc.). If I define ft `tutor` for MY lessons, THEIR ftplugin kicks in: `buftype=nofile` makes the buffer non-writeable-ish (buftype=nofile buffers can still be modified in memory but can't be written), concealcursor, tutor mappings via `tutor#SetNormalMappings()`, plus syntax expecting markdown format with `~~~` code fences and `**bold**` etc.

2. Their `:Tutor` (nvim) → `tutor#TutorCmd` opens `$VIMRUNTIME/tutor.tutor`-style markdown interactive tutorials and expects `.tutor.json` metadata.

Options:

- **A) Fight/coexist with ft=tutor**: Set my own distinct filetype, e.g. `vimtutor`, so the stock tutor ftplugin/syntax never engages. I then write MY ftplugin/vimtutor.vim + syntax/vimtutor.vim. Clean separation. The `:Tutor` command override: mine loaded later via rtp+= overrides with `command!`. Works in both. And I use classic `~`-border format (like original vimtutor), NOT markdown — simple, retro, no conceal weirdness. ft=vimtutor. 

- **B) Adopt the runtime tutor format (markdown .tutor files)**: leverage their concealing/marks/interactive checks — but that format requires JSON metadata for interactivity, and the runtime tutor is fairly rigid; also writing metadata JSON for 13 lessons is a big lift. And it engages their mappings.

A is clearly better: full control, simpler, robust. My lessons keep the beloved classic `~` look (nostalgia!) — that's a feature, not a bug. The classic format is what the user remembers ("back in the day").

I'll use extension `.tut`? Hmm `.tvt`? Let me use `*.vimtutor` — unambiguous, self-documenting. ft=vimtutor.

- To dodge their `plugin/tutor.vim`'s tutor runtime plugin entirely (it only defines command + autocommands? plugin file only defines :Tutor command + maybe some autocmd), fine: our rtp+= append means our `command!` wins in both editors. =  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 1: Windows and Splits                        =
================================================================================

  A window is a viewport onto a buffer. A split gives you a second window,
  usually showing the same or a related file at the same time. You will use
  splits constantly: file on the left, test on the right; code and its
  documentation; a buffer and its git blame.

  1. Open a fresh scratch window with :new (empty buffer, horizontal split)
     ~ Try it now -- type :new<Enter> on the line below and keep both:
     ~
     ~      +-----------------------------+
     ~      | lesson 1 (this text)        |
     ~      +-----------------------------+
     ~      | [No Name]                   |
     ~      +-----------------------------+
     ~
     ~ Close the empty window again with Ctrl-W c (or :q).

  2. Vertical splits are the everyday ones. Practice on the line below:
     ~
     ~  a. :vsplit<Enter>            split the window in half, left/right
     ~  b. Ctrl-W w                  hop to the other window (w = window)
     ~  c. Ctrl-W h  /  Ctrl-W l     go to LEFT / RIGHT window
     ~  d. :only<Enter>              close every other window (Ctrl-W o)
     ~
     ~ Do a :vsplit and navigate until it feels automatic, then tidy up
     ~ with :only.

  3. Windows with content:
     ~
     ~  :e 02-<Tab>                 edit the next lesson in THIS window
     ~  :vsplit 02-<Tab>            edit another file in a NEW split
     ~  :new                        empty window, bottom half
     ~  :vnew                       empty window, right half
     ~
     ~ Make a mess: two windows on this lesson and one on lesson 2. The
     ~ same buffer may show in many windows. Clean up with :only.

  4. Moving around fast:
     ~
     ~  Ctrl-W h j k l              move left / down / up / right
     ~  Ctrl-W w                    cycle through all windows
     ~  Ctrl-W p                    previous window (the one you left)
     ~  2 Ctrl-W w                  jump two windows ahead (count works)
     ~
     ~ Split twice and hop a lap. Note that hjkl with Ctrl-W -- not the
     ~ Ctrl-W h alone -- is what most Vim users actually type.

  5. Rearranging (all with Ctrl-W):
     ~
     ~  H J K L                     shove the window to the far edge
     ~  r                           rotate window positions
     ~  x                           swap two windows
     ~  T                           tear this window out to a new TAB
     ~
     ~ Try Ctrl-W K then Ctrl-W J -- you get a full-width "banner" layout.
     ~ You will meet Ctrl-W T again in Lesson 2.

     ~  :resize 12                  this window 12 lines tall

=  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 2: Buffers and Tabs -- The Mental Model      =
================================================================================

  THE THREE-LEVEL MODEL (draw it in your head before every "where am I" doubt)

  ~   buffer   one in-memory copy of a file's text  (you are in buffer
  ~            00-... right now -- see it with :ls)
  ~   window   a viewport onto ONE buffer; splits show 2+ buffers at once
  ~   tab      a complete LAYOUT of windows -- a spare workbench, not "pages"

  ~      +-------------+-----------+   files -- most are in memory but do
  ~      | buffer      | buffer    |   NOT appear in any window. That is
  ~      | 00-index    | 01-splits |   normal! Windows are views; buffers
  ~      +-------------+-----------+   are the content.

  1. See what is loaded:

     ~  :ls<Enter>                  list buffers: number, state, name
     ~  :ls!<Enter>                 include the hidden/system ones too
     ~
     ~ State flags you will meet: a=active, h=hidden, %=current, #=alternate

     ~  :b 05-<Tab>                 fuzzy prefix + Tab completion, enter
     ~  :bn  /  :bp                 next / previous buffer in the list
     ~  :b#                         jump to the alternate buffer
     ~  Ctrl-6  (alias Ctrl-^)      same jump, no command line needed
     ~
     ~ Toggle between THIS lesson and another with Ctrl-6 a few times --
     ~ that is the single most-used buffer key in real life.

     ~  :bd                         delete THIS buffer from the list
     ~  :bd 02-<Tab>                delete a specific one by pattern

================================================================================
=  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 1: Windows and Splits                        =
================================================================================

  A window is a viewport onto a buffer. A split gives you a second
  window -- usually the same or a related file at the same time. You
  will use splits constantly: code on the left, its tests on the right,
  the file on top and its documentation below.

  1. Your first split, in and out:
     ~
     ~  Type :new<Enter> on the line below: a scratch buffer opens below
     ~  this one. Look, then close it with Ctrl-W c (or :q).
     ~
     ~        +---------------------------------------+
     ~        | lesson 1 (this text)                  |
     ~        +---------------------------------------+
     ~        | [No Name]                             |
     ~        +---------------------------------------+

  2. Vertical splits -- the everyday ones. Practice below:
     ~
     ~  :vsplit<Enter>        split left/right showing this buffer twice
     ~  Ctrl-W w              hop to the other window (w = window)
     ~  Ctrl-W h / Ctrl-W l   go to the LEFT / RIGHT window
     ~  :only<Enter>          close every other window (alias Ctrl-W o)
     ~
     ~ Split, navigate a few times, then tidy up with :only.

  3. Windows with content:
     ~
     ~  :e 03-<Tab>           edit another lesson in THIS window
     ~  :vsplit 03-<Tab>      ...or in a NEW split instead
     ~  :new                  a new empty window below (horizontal)
     ~  :vnew                 a new empty window to the right
     ~
     ~ Make a mess: two windows on this lesson plus one on lesson 3.
     ~ The same buffer may appear in many windows at once. Clean up
     ~ with :only.

  4. Moving fast between windows (all Ctrl-W chords):
     ~
     ~  Ctrl-W h j k l        move left / down / up / right
     ~  Ctrl-W w              cycle through all windows
     ~  Ctrl-W p              previous window -- the one you just left
     ~  2 Ctrl-W w            two windows ahead (counts compose)

  5. Rearranging, all with Ctrl-W:
     ~
     ~  H J K L               shove the window hard left/down/up/right
     ~  r                     rotate window positions
     ~  x                     exchange this window with the next one
     ~  T                     tear this window out into a new TAB
     ~
     ~ Try Ctrl-W K then Ctrl-W J: you get a banner-style layout. You
     ~ will meet Ctrl-W T again in Lesson 2.

  6. Sizes:
     ~
     ~  Ctrl-W +   Ctrl-W -   grow / shrink the HEIGHT by one line
     ~  Ctrl-W >   Ctrl-W <   widen / narrow by one column
     ~  Ctrl-W _              maximize height     Ctrl-W |  max width
     ~  Ctrl-W =              equalize every split -- the tidy-up key
     ~  :resize 12            this window exactly 12 lines tall
     ~  :vertical resize 90   this window exactly 90 columns wide
     ~
     ~ Where do NEW splits land? Two options decide:
     ~        :set splitbelow?    :set splitright?
     ~ (the trailing ? prints the current value). Your shared config
     ~ turns both on, so :new and :vnew appear below and to the right,
     ~ where your eyes already are.

  7. A real workflow, start to finish:
     ~
     ~  :vsplit demo/<Enter>   the built-in file explorer (netrw) opens
     ~                         in the left half -- Lesson 10 teaches it
     ~  Press v on a file name to open it in the right half (or o for a
     ~  horizontal split). Hop with Ctrl-W h / Ctrl-W l. Finish with
     ~  Ctrl-W = to equalize.

  NOTE: Everything in this lesson is plain, built-in Vim -- identical in
  Vim and Neovim, no plugins involved.

  SUMMARY -- Lesson 1

  ~ :split :vsplit :new :vnew   create windows (Ctrl-W s v n are twins)
  ~ Ctrl-W h j k l w p          move between windows
  ~ Ctrl-W H J K L r x T        reposition, rotate, swap, tear to tab
  ~ Ctrl-W c q o                close / quit / keep only this window
  ~ Ctrl-W + - = _ | < >        resize and equalize
  ~ :resize N :vertical resize  exact sizes
  ~ :set splitbelow splitright  where new splits appear

================================================================================

================================================================================
=  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 2: Buffers and Tabs, the Mental Model        =
================================================================================

  THE THREE-LEVEL MODEL -- picture this before every "where am I?" doubt

  ~  buffer   one in-memory copy of a file's text. All 14 lessons plus
  ~           the demo files are loaded right now -- see the list with
  ~           :ls. Most of them appear NOWHERE: that is normal. Windows
  ~           are views; buffers are the content.
  ~  window   a viewport onto ONE buffer; splits show 2+ at a time
  ~  tab      one complete LAYOUT of windows -- a spare workbench,
  ~           not a stack of "pages" like in a GUI editor

  ~      tab 1:                    +-----------+ +-------------+
  ~      a layout of windows       | buffer 00 | | buffer 01   |
  ~      showing two of the        | (index)   | | (splits)    |
  ~      17 in-memory buffers      +-----------+ +-------------+

  1. See what is loaded:
     ~
     ~  :ls<Enter>             list buffers: number, state, name
     ~  :ls!<Enter>            also the unlisted/hidden ones
     ~
     ~ State letters you will meet: a = active (shown), h = hidden
     ~ (loaded, not shown), % = this window's buffer, # = alternate -- 
     ~ the one you came from.

  2. Switching -- the daily bread:
     ~
     ~  :b 05-<Tab>            type a prefix, Tab completes, Enter jumps
     ~  :bn  /  :bp            next / previous buffer in the list
     ~  :b#                    jump to the alternate buffer
     ~  Ctrl-6  (Ctrl-^)       same jump as :b#, without the command line
     ~
     ~ Toggle between this lesson and another with Ctrl-6 a few times.
     ~ This is the single most-used buffer key in real work.

  3. Open, close, and the "hidden" setting:
     ~
     ~  :e 03-<Tab>            load a buffer into the CURRENT window
     ~  :vsplit 04-<Tab>       load one into a NEW window instead
     ~  :bd                    delete this buffer from the list
     ~  :bd!                   ...even if it has unsaved changes
     ~
     ~ NOTE: 'hidden' is ON in your shared config, so switching away
     ~ from an edited buffer no longer demands a save first. :ls marks
     ~ such buffers with + or a in the state column. :bd on an edited
     ~ buffer still complains -- that complaint protects you; use :bd!
     ~ only when you mean it.

  4. One window per buffer:
     ~
     ~  :ball                  a window for every listed buffer
     ~  :vertical ball         the same, side by side (wide screens!)
     ~  Ctrl-W o               back to one window only
     ~
     ~ Try :vertical ball -- the famous "everything at once" view.
     ~ Windows appear in buffer-number order, top-to-bottom on the
     ~ left, continuing to the right.

  5. Loop over all of them:
     ~
     ~  :bufdo set list?       run a command in every loaded buffer
     ~  :windo echo winnr()    ...or in every window
     ~
     ~ :bufdo and :windo show up everywhere in advanced usage. Lesson 6
     ~ adds :argdo (files) and :cfdo (quickfix results).

  6. TABS = window layouts. Build two workbenches:
     ~
     ~  :tabnew                a new tab page with an empty scratch
     ~  :tabnew 04-<Tab>       open lesson 4 in a brand-new tab
     ~  gt / gT                next / previous tab
     ~  2gt                    go to tab 2 (counts work here too)
     ~  :tabs                  list every tab and its windows
     ~  :tabclose              close this tab      :tabonly keep only it
     ~
     ~ A common layout: one tab for source, one for tests, one for the
     ~ terminal (Lesson 11), one for netrw. Tabs are cheap; don't hoard
     ~ splits -- spread work across tabs instead.

  7. Shuffling windows and tabs around:
     ~
     ~  Ctrl-W T               move THIS window out to a new tab
     ~  :tabmove 0             reorder -- :tabm 0 makes it the first
     ~  :tabdo %s/TODO/DONE/g  run a command in every tab's buffer

  NOTE: Buffers created by :Tutor are scratch copies of lesson files in
  a temp folder. :bd on them is always safe.

  SUMMARY -- Lesson 2

  ~ :ls :b :bn :bp :b# Ctrl-6     list and switch buffers
  ~ :e file :vsplit file :bd [!]  load / close buffers
  ~ :ball :vertical ball          one window per buffer
  ~ :bufdo :windo                 act on all buffers / windows
  ~ :tabnew gt gT Ngt :tabs       tab pages are window layouts
  ~ :tabclose :tabonly :tabmove   manipulate tabs
  ~ Ctrl-W T                      window -> its own tab

================================================================================

================================================================================
=  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 3: Registers -- Yank, Delete, Put            =
================================================================================

  Every yank (y), delete (d) and change (c) writes its text into a
  register. The obvious one is the unnamed register, " in :reg. But
  there are 26 named registers, 10 numbered ones, and a handful of
  special slots. Knowing which is which turns your clipboard into a
  precision tool instead of a lottery.

  1. Inspect the machinery:
     ~
     ~  Put the cursor on the word  --->  register
     ~  and yank it with yiw. Now type :reg<Enter> and find the unnamed
     ~  register (") holding the word. Then note the rules:
     ~
     ~  ~ y yank        fills  "  AND  "0   (the yank register)
     ~  ~ d c           fill   "  AND  "1   (older deletes shift to "2.."9)
     ~  ~ x s dd cC     on one small piece also fill "-"  (small delete)

  2. The yank register survives intervening deletes:
     ~
     ~      --->  survivor
     ~      --->  deleted
     ~
     ~  yiw survivor        ("0 and " = "survivor")
     ~  j
     ~  daw                 (" = "deleted", but "0 STILL = "survivor")
     ~  p                   pastes "deleted" from the unnamed register
     ~  "0p                 pastes "survivor" from the YANK register
     ~
     ~ That is the trick: "0p pastes your last yank no matter how much
     ~ deleting happened in between. No re-yank, no loss.

  3. Named registers "a-"z -- your own slots:
     ~
     ~      --->  alpha beta gamma
     ~
     ~  "ayy                yank THIS line into register a
     ~  "byiw  and  "cyiw   yank beta and gamma into b and c
     ~  Move to the end of the buffer, on its last line type:
     ~      "bp<Esc>"cp<Esc>"ap<Esc>
     ~  and reassemble the words in a new order. Check with :reg abc.
     ~
     ~ APPEND versions (capital letter): "Ayy appends ANOTHER LINE to
     ~ register a instead of replacing it. Collect lines one by one,
     ~ then paste the lot with "ap -- the classic "build a list" trick.

  4. The blackhole register "_ -- delete without remembering:
     ~
     ~  "_diw       deletes a word and writes NOTHING anywhere
     ~  "_dd        deletes lines without clobbering your paste slot
     ~
     ~ Use it when you have valuable text parked in " and still need
     ~ quick deleting. Deleting should never cost you your clipboard.

  5. The system clipboard registers "+ and "*:
     ~
     ~  :echo has('clipboard')        does THIS editor carry them?
     ~
     ~  ~ In Neovim they work when a provider is found (xclip /
     ~  ~ wl-clipboard on Wayland, pbcopy on macOS). :checkhealth tells.
     ~  ~ In Vim they need a build compiled WITH the X clipboard --
     ~  ~ Debian's default `vim` package usually lacks it; install the
     ~  ~ `vim-gtk3` package and /usr/bin/vim regains +clipboard.
     ~
     ~  With them working:  "+y copies the selection to the OS clipboard,
     ~  "+p pastes from it. :set clipboard=unnamed makes " and "+" ONE
     ~  register (every d/y/p crosses into the OS clipboard). Powerful --
     ~  and a big muscle-memory change, so flip it consciously.

  6. Ex-mode register commands worth knowing:
     ~
     ~  :put a                    paste register a below this line
     ~  :'<,'>normal "ap          (after V) paste "a at every line
     ~  :echo @a                  show me what is in register a
     ~  :help registers<Enter>    the full story when you want it

  SUMMARY -- Lesson 3

  ~ y d c fill " the unnamed      p P paste it back
  ~ "0                            last yank: "0p survives deleting
  ~ "1-9  and  "-                 recent big deletes / small deletes
  ~ "a-"z  "A-"Z                  named slots; capitals APPEND
  ~ "_                            blackhole: delete without storing
  ~ "+ "*                         system clipboards (provider/build!)
  ~ :reg "ap "Ayy :put a          inspect and use registers in Ex mode
  ~ :set clipboard=unnamed        merge OS clipboard with "

================================================================================

================================================================================
=  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 4: Macros -- Recorded Power                  =
================================================================================

  A macro is a NORMAL MODE recording stored in a register. You record a
  small edit once, then replay it on similar lines. This is the single
  biggest productivity leap Vim offers for repetitive edits -- and the
  reason q is NOT mapped to quit anywhere in this tutor.

  1. The canonical demo -- numbering lines with Ctrl-A:
     ~
     ~  The block below has five identical lines. Stand on the digit of
     ~  the FIRST line, then record:
     ~
     ~      ~ item 1
     ~      ~ item 1
     ~      ~ item 1
     ~      ~ item 1
     ~      ~ item 1
     ~
     ~    Step 1:  q a          start recording into register a
     ~    Step 2:  Ctrl-A       bump 1 -> 2  (on this line only)
     ~    Step 3:  j            down to the next identically-shaped line
     ~    Step 4:  q            stop recording
     ~
     ~    Step 5:  @a           replay once              (line 2 -> 3)
     ~    Step 6:  @@           replay the LAST macro    (line 3 -> 4)
     ~    Step 7:  @@           again                    (line 4 -> 5)
     ~
     ~  Ctrl-A increases the number under the cursor (Ctrl-X decreases).
     ~  The macro is "change this digit, go down" -- which is why it
     ~  self-propagates. :reg a shows the tiny recording.

  2. Replays with counts -- and a clean slate:
     ~
     ~  Undo all of it:  u u u u  or simply  :undo 0<Enter>
     ~  Stand on the first 1 again and type  4@a<Enter>
     ~  Counts before @ replay it that many times. 4@a does the whole
     ~  column in one press.

  3. A text editing macro from start to finish:
     ~
     ~  Turn EVERY line below into a checked box: " [x] some words here "
     ~
     ~      ~ some words here
     ~      ~ some words here too
     ~      ~ yet some words again
     ~
     ~  Stand on the first line (column zero), then record exactly:

     ~    q a          record into a
     ~    I            insert at the first non-blank of THIS line
     ~    [x]<Space>   type those four characters literally
     ~    Esc          back to normal mode -- macro steps need it
     ~    j            down one line, so replays land on the next
     ~    q            stop
     ~
     ~    2@a          ...and the remaining two lines convert at once.

  4. Macros over visual selections with :normal:
     ~
     ~  Select the three lines with V (Lesson 5 has the full tour),
     ~  then run:

     ~    :'<,'>normal @a<Enter>

     ~  :normal plays keys AS IF TYPED, once per selected line -- with
     ~  @a inside, that applies the macro to any range you like, not
     ~  just to whatever  j  happens to reach. (gv reselects the last
     ~  visual selection afterwards.)

  5. Fixing a macro by editing the register:
     ~
     ~  Recording is only the START. The macro lives in a register, so
     ~  you can read and rewrite it:

     ~    :put a<Enter>          paste register a as plain text here
     ~    Edit that line: change j to 0, or add a second j...
     ~    :let @a = getline('.')      capture the whole line back
     ~    @a                          the NEW macro, in action
     ~
     ~  (getline('.') works for single-line macros. Multi-line ones you
     ~  set directly: :let @a = "i[x] \<Esc>j"  -- quote quotes as \".)

  6. Appending to a recording:
     ~
     ~  q A          record MORE keys, appended to register a
     ~  ... q        stop
     ~
     ~  @a now does the old steps, then the new ones. Use it when a
     ~  macro "almost" fits: extend, don't re-record.

  REMEMBER: q starts a recording in normal mode; :q quits a window. Two
  different verbs, no conflict in this tutor.

  SUMMARY -- Lesson 4

  ~ q{register} ... q     record / stop recording (qA appends)
  ~ @a  @@  3@a           run it, re-run it, run it N times
  ~ :'<,'>normal @a       run once per line of a visual range
  ~ :put a :echo @a       read the raw keystrokes
  ~ :let @a = getline('.')  rewrite single-line macros after editing
  ~ :reg                  macros are just registers -- peek any time
  ~ q is record, :q is quit -- never map q away in a real config

================================================================================

================================================================================
=  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 5: Visual Modes and Text Objects             =
================================================================================

  Visual mode is not about "selecting" -- it is about applying an
  operator to text by MEANING: a word, a paragraph, a quoted string, a
  block of lines -- without counting characters. Learn the objects and
  your edits stop being measured in keystrokes.

  1. The three visual modes:
     ~
     ~   v          character-wise (the everyday one)
     ~   V          line-wise
     ~   Ctrl-V     block-wise -- a RECTANGLE, column edits included
     ~   gv         reselect the last selection whenever you need it
     ~
     ~ Enter each mode on the line below, wave the cursor around, exit
     ~ with Esc, watch the mode name change in the status line.
     ~
     ~      --->  try me here

  2. Block-visual magic -- Ctrl-V pays for this whole lesson:
     ~
     ~  Ctrl-V j j j over the leading spaces of the block below makes a
     ~  4-line rectangle. With it selected:
     ~
     ~    I # <Esc>        insert at the START of every line at once
     ~    u                (undo), then try the rest:
     ~    A  end<Esc>      append at the END of every line at once
     ~    c<Esc>           hollow the block: change all lines together
     ~    ~                flip the case of the whole selection
     ~    o                move opposite corner, O move opposite side
     ~    r*               replace every char of the block with *
     ~
     ~      ~ alpha one
     ~      ~ alpha two
     ~      ~ alpha three
     ~      ~ alpha four

  3. Visual mode writes its own Ex ranges:
     ~
     ~  Select two or three lines with V j, then:
     ~
     ~    :sort<Enter>          sorts only the selected lines (built in!)
     ~    :s/alpha/BETA/<Enter> the range :'<,'> is pre-typed for you
     ~    :normal A;<Enter>     normal-mode keys per selected line
     ~    J                     join the selected lines (in V mode)
     ~
     ~ Those :'<,'> ranges can also be typed by hand in the command line.

  4. TEXT OBJECTS -- operator + i|a + object:
     ~
     ~   i = inner, JUST the object      a = "a-round", object + padding
     ~
     ~   iw  aw     word, with or without its trailing space
     ~   i(  a(     inside / around parentheses   (ib ab are aliases)
     ~   i{  a{     inside / around a code block (iB aB likewise)
     ~   i"  a"     inside / around double quotes (' ` too)
     ~   ip  ap     inside / around a paragraph
     ~   it  at     inside / around an XML-ish tag (it = inner tag)
     ~
     ~  Practice on the line  --->  call(alpha_value, "text here")
     ~
     ~    ci(               change everything inside the parentheses
     ~    da"               delete the string INCLUDING its quotes
     ~    va(               select around the parens, then u to undo
     ~    2i)               count UP the nesting: two paren levels in
     ~
     ~  The general shape is always: operator, i/a, object. d a p
     ~  deletes a paragraph, y i " yanks a string's contents -- hundreds
     ~  of combinations, one grammar.

  5. The dot command, one level up:
     ~
     ~  ciwWORD<Esc>   change one word; find the next occurrence with n
     ~  .              ...and press dot -- the SAME edit again, instantly
     ~
     ~ ciw + n + . is often faster than any regex. It is the partner of
     ~ macros: dot for "again here", @a for "here and the next three".

  6. Bonus -- vim-surround is installed for you (see Lesson 9):
     ~
     ~  On the line  --->  "just text"
     ~
     ~    cs"'                 change surrounding " to '
     ~    cs'`<                to backticks, then to tags: c s ' <
     ~    ds"                  delete the surrounding quotes
     ~    ysiw"                wrap the word under cursor in quotes
     ~    S"                   in VISUAL: wrap the selection in "
     ~
     ~ Works for (), {}, and t for tags: :help surround when curious.

  SUMMARY -- Lesson 5

  ~ v V Ctrl-V gv          three visual modes + reselect
  ~ o O                    move the selection's ends
  ~ I A c ~ r in block mode   column edits that stick together
  ~ :sort :'<,'>s          visual modes pre-type ranges for you
  ~ i/a + iw aw i( i{ i" ip it   objects by meaning
  ~ 2i)                    counts reach through nesting
  ~ ciw ... n ... .         dot as the lightweight macro
  ~ cs ds ysiw S            surround: edit the wrapper, not the text

================================================================================

================================================================================
=  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 6: Search, :s, :global, Quickfix             =
================================================================================

  Searching and replacing is where Vim either feels clumsy or feels
  like a superpower. The difference is knowing: flags on :s, very-magic
  regexes, :global, and using the quickfix list to edit MANY files at
  once. Your shared config already sets -- :set ignorecase smartcase?

  1. The search loop:
     ~
     ~   /pattern<Enter>   search forward; ? backward; n N next/prev hit
     ~   *                 search the word under the cursor (whole word)
     ~   :noh              clear the highlighting until the next search
     ~   :set hlsearch!    turn highlighting off for real
     ~
     ~ Search for alpha in this lesson, hop around with n, N, come back
     ~ with Ctrl-O. That jumplist integration is part of the point.

  2. :s -- the flags you will actually use:
     ~
     ~   :%s/alpha/BETA/g       whole file, every hit per line
     ~   :%s/alpha/BETA/gi      ...case-insensitive (I forces sensitive)
     ~   :%s/alpha/BETA/gc      CONFIRM each hit: y n a q l keys below
     ~   :'<,'>s/alpha/BETA/g   only the visually selected lines
     ~   :&&                    repeat the last :s exactly (keeps flags)
     ~   :%s//BETA/g            SEARCH half empty = reuse your last /search
     ~   :%s/alpha//gd          g + d: delete the whole line of each hit? 
     ~                          (d flag joins the rest of the line -- see
     ~                          :h s_flags before trusting it in real code)
     ~
     ~ At the c-confirm prompt: y = yes, n = no, a = yes-to-all-here,
     ~ l = last one then stop, q = quit. Ctrl-E / Ctrl-Y scroll around
     ~ while deciding.

  3. Very magic -- regexes that read like other tools:
     ~
     ~   In Vim's default magic, ( ) | + ? must be BACKSLASHED. Prefix
     ~   \v ("very magic") and they are literal-meaning again:
     ~
     ~     :%s/\v(alpha_value|beta_value)/\1_v2/g     \1 \2 = capture groups
     ~     :%s/\vdate=\zs\d\ze/2026/   \zs starts the match AFTER 'date=',
     ~                                 \ze ends it -- replace only digits
     ~
     ~   Practice the \v form on this lesson's own text: count matches
     ~   FIRST with the n flag:  :%s/\v(alpha)+//gn<Enter>  (no change!)

  4. :global -- run an Ex command on every matching line:
     ~
     ~   :g/TODO/t$              copy every TODO line to the buffer end
     ~   :g/^#/d                 delete every line starting with #
     ~   :v/TODO/d               the INVERSE: delete lines WITHOUT it
     ~   :g/;/normal A           run normal-mode keys per matching line
     ~   :g//                    no pattern = reuse the last search
     ~
     ~   :g is nearly a programming language (help :g). These four idioms
     ~   cover 90% of daily use.

  5. The quickfix list -- searching across MANY files:
     ~
     ~   :cd %:p:h               make the scratch folder the working dir
     ~   :vimgrep /TODO/j **/*   collect matches from every file (j: don't
     ~                           jump to the first hit yet)
     ~   :copen                  the quickfix window -- every hit, file:line
     ~   <Enter> in the list     jump to that hit
     ~   :cn :cp :cc 3           next / previous / entry number 3
     ~   :cclose                 close the window
     ~
     ~   Bulk-edit the HITS, not whole files:
     ~
     ~   :cfdo %s/TODO/NOTE~/gc  substitute in every file that had hits
     ~   :cfdo update            save each file that changed
     ~   :cdo %s/TODO/x/g        (per-ENTRY variant, both editors have it)
     ~
     ~ NOTE: **/* is the "all files, all subdirectories" glob. :vimgrep
     ~ also accepts shell-style patterns for one directory.

  6. Command-line helpers for heavy regex work:
     ~
     ~   q/                      your search HISTORY as an editable buffer
     ~   q:                      ...same for commands (edit, Enter = run)
     ~   Ctrl-R Ctrl-W           paste the word under cursor into cmdline
     ~   Ctrl-R /                paste the last search pattern into cmdline
     ~   :%s/TODO//gn            COUNT occurrences (n flag: report, no edit)
     ~
     ~  For gnarly patterns, build them inside q/ where editing is easy,
     ~  then reuse from the cmdline with Ctrl-R /.

  SUMMARY -- Lesson 6

  ~ * # n N :noh hlsearch         basic search loop + highlighting
  ~ :%s/old/new/g  gi gc  :&&     substitutes with the flags that matter
  ~ :'<,'>s                       range from visual selection
  ~ \v \zs \ze                    very magic + match-edge pinning
  ~ :g/pat/cmd :v/pat/d           global: act per matching line
  ~ :vimgrep :copen :cn :cc 3     quickfix across files
  ~ :cfdo :cdo :cfdo update       edit every hit, save what changed
  ~ q: q/ Ctrl-R Ctrl-W Ctrl-R /  cmdline as a first-class editor

================================================================================

================================================================================
=  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 7: Marks and Jumps                           =
================================================================================

  Real navigation is not cursor-walking -- it is remembering places and
  moving in big, meaningful steps. Two systems do this: marks (you set
  them) and the jumplist (Vim tracks it for you). Between classes at
  school and jumplist ping-pong, you will rarely page through a file
  line-by-line again.

  1. Marks -- names for places:
     ~
     ~   m a--z              set a mark in THIS buffer (ma, mm, ...)
     ~   m A--Z              a GLOBAL mark: survives switching files!
     ~   ' a                 jump to mark a, start of line
     ~   ` a                 jump to mark a, EXACT row and column
     ~   :marks              list all marks in this session
     ~   :delm a b c         delete specific marks (:delm! = a-z)
     ~
     ~ Set a mark m with mm here, wander down, return with 'm.
     ~ Marks Vim sets by itself:
     ~
     ~   ''                  where you were before the last jump
     ~   ``                  ...exact position (the pair you'll type most)
     ~   `.                  position of the last change
     ~   `^                  where insert mode was left

  2. The jumplist -- Ctrl-O and Ctrl-I:
     ~
     ~   Ctrl-O              BACK through every jump you made
     ~   Ctrl-I              FORWARD again (Tab too, unless remapped)
     ~   3 Ctrl-O            three jumps back, one press
     ~   :jumps              the whole trail with positions
     ~
     ~ What counts as a jump: gg, G, /, ?, n, N, {, }, (, ), %, and
     ~ mark jumps. Plain h j k l and w e b do NOT -- the trail stays
     ~ meaningful instead of recording every step.

  3. A two-buffer ping-pong with global marks:
     ~
     ~   mA                  drop GLOBAL mark A on this lesson
     ~   :e 08-<Tab>         open lesson 8 in this window
     ~   mB                  drop global mark B there
     ~   `A `B `A `B         bounce between two files at exact spots
     ~   Ctrl-O              notice: the jumplist tracked the file hops
     ~
     ~ Global marks persist across sessions too (via viminfo/shada) --
     ~ keep a few reserved: A project todo, B the test file, and so on.

  4. The command window -- history as an editable buffer:
     ~
     ~   q:                  your COMMAND history in a split window
     ~   q/                  your SEARCH history likewise
     ~   Edit any line (regexes included!), press <Enter> to run it
     ~   :q                  close the window without running anything
     ~
     ~ The unsung hero for long :s commands: open q:, fish out the last
     ~ big substitute, edit just the pattern, Enter.

  5. Structural motions -- move by shape, not by scroll:
     ~
     ~   %                   jump to the matching ( [ { under the cursor
     ~   ]m ]M               next / previous start-of-method
     ~   [m [M               same, backwards
     ~   [[ ]]               previous / next section (C-like code)
     ~   ]#                  previous? next #if/#else/#endif boundary
     ~   gd gD               local / global declaration of word under cursor
     ~
     ~ With a language server (Lesson 12, coc.nvim) gd becomes semantic:
     ~ a true definition jump across files, recorded in the same
     ~ jumplist, Ctrl-O brings you home.

  SUMMARY -- Lesson 7

  ~ m a  m A  ' a  ` a    marks: local, global, linewise, exact
  ~ ''  ``  `.  `^        the free ones: back, back-exact, change, insert
  ~ :marks :delm          list and delete marks
  ~ Ctrl-O Ctrl-I :jumps  the jumplist: big-step history
  ~ q: q/ :q              command window -- history you can edit
  ~ % ]m [[ gd gD         structural motions (LSP upgrades gd)

================================================================================

=  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 8: Folds                                     =
================================================================================

  Folds hide text you are not currently caring about: bodies of
  functions you are not editing, blocks of config, long comments. The
  text is never deleted -- a fold is pure VIEWPORT metadata, exactly
  like a window is.

  1. Fold by indentation -- works here, works in any indented code:
     ~
     ~   :set foldmethod=indent<Enter>
     ~   z M                  close everything (Mnemonic: More folds)
     ~   Stand inside the block below and:
     ~     z o                open ONE level
     ~     z c                close again
     ~     z a                toggle the fold you are in
     ~   z R                  Reduce the folds: open everything
     ~
     ~      ~ level one
     ~      ~   level two
     ~      ~     level three
     ~      ~   level two
     ~      ~ level one

  2. Manual folds -- draw your own:
     ~
     ~   :set foldmethod=manual<Enter>
     ~   z f motion           create a fold (zfap = fold this paragraph)
     ~   Select 3 lines with V, then zf -- a fold from your selection
     ~   z F                  fold a fixed number of lines from here
     ~   :1,4fold             any Ex range folds too
     ~   z d                  delete THIS fold definition
     ~   z E                  delete ALL folds in the buffer
     ~
     ~ zf, zF, zd, zE shape the fold STRUCTURE. The text is untouched.

  3. Folding by syntax or expression:
     ~
     ~   :set foldmethod=syntax    when a syntax file provides fold
     ~                             regions (many language plugins do)
     ~   :set foldmethod=expr      follow any expression -- this is how
     ~                             Neovim + treesitter folds are wired in
     ~                             modern configs
     ~
     ~ Your config leaves folding OFF by default (foldmethod=manual, no
     ~ folds open). Turn indent-folding on for good by adding
     ~ set foldmethod=indent to your vimrc -- see Lesson 9.

  4. The command set at a glance:
     ~
     ~   z o z c z a          open / close / toggle, the fold at cursor
     ~   z O z C z A          the same, recursively (whole nest)
     ~   z R z M              open all / close all
     ~   z v                  open just enough to show the cursor
     ~   [z  ]z               top / bottom of the current open fold
     ~   z j z k              down / up to the next fold's start
     ~
     ~ Counts compose: 3zo opens three levels deep at once.

  5. Options that make folds pleasant:
     ~
     ~   :set foldlevel=99    start with everything open, close by hand
     ~   :set foldnestmax=3   no folds nested deeper than 3
     ~   :set foldminlines=1  refuse to fold single lines
     ~   :set foldcolumn=3    a gutter strip showing fold state, per line
     ~   :h fold-commands     the full reference

  SUMMARY -- Lesson 8

  ~ :set foldmethod=...   indent, manual, syntax, expr (per-plugin)
  ~ zf zF zd zE           define folds from selections, ranges, motion
  ~ zo zc za  zO zC zA    open / close / toggle, plain and recursive
  ~ zR zM                 open or close the world
  ~ [z ]z zj zk           navigate fold structure
  ~ foldlevel foldcolumn  make folds visible and predictable

================================================================================

=  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 9: Config, Mappings, Plugins, Colorschemes   =
================================================================================

  Where YOUR configuration lives:

  ~  Vim:       ~/.vimrc      Neovim: ~/.config/nvim/init.vim
  ~
  ~ setup.sh created both with a two-line job: source one shared file
  ~ so a single configuration serves both editors:
  ~
  ~     ~/.local/share/vimtutor/config/vimrc.common
  ~
  ~ Change options in the shared file, or add your own below it -- your
  ~ editor's own init file is the right place for personal overrides,
  ~ because setup.sh must never have to rewrite it.

  1. Find it every time, free of charge:
     ~
     ~   :e $MYVIMRC            open YOUR active init file
     ~   :echo $MYVIMRC         or just see its path
     ~   Follow the source line to the shared config, then:
     ~   :source $MYVIMRC       reload after editing (alias :so %)

  2. Options worth knowing cold:
     ~
     ~   :options<Enter>     the built-in browse-every-option page
     ~   :set nu? rnu?       number + relativenumber: relative digits are
     ~                       what makes  d3j  countable at a glance
     ~   :set hidden?        switch buffers without saving first
     ~   :set undodir?       plus 'undofile' -- history survives restarts
     ~   :set path?          what :find searches (Lesson 10 extends it)
     ~   :set so?            scrolloff: 8 lines of context at the edge
     ~   :set wildmenu?      the cmdline completion menu below :e <Tab>

  3. Mappings -- and the nnoremap rule:
     ~
     ~   :nnoremap <leader>t :tabnew<Enter>          define one, live!
     ~   Press <Space>t right now -- a new tab opens.
     ~   :nmap <leader>t      ...and :nmap shows what it points at
     ~
     ~   The rule: map RECURSIVE variants (map, nmap) can trigger other
     ~   mappings -- an accident-prone chain. Always define with the
     ~   non-recursive set:  nnoremap inoremap vnoremap xnoremap.
     ~
     ~   <leader> is your personal prefix. The shared config sets
     ~   let mapleader = " "  (the space bar). :echo mapleader to check.
     ~   Vim waits a moment for the next key: :set timeoutlen?

  4. Plugins managed IN the editor -- vim-plug:
     ~
     ~   :PlugStatus            what is installed, what is missing
     ~   :PlugInstall           fetch everything missing (first run!)
     ~   :PlugUpdate            update the installed ones
     ~   :PlugClean             remove plugins no longer in the config
     ~
     ~   The :Plug lines live in the shared config under the comment
     ~   "Plugins via vim-plug"; clones land in plugged/ beside it.
     ~   What the reasonable defaults give you:
     ~
     ~  ~ coc.nvim                    completion + LSP client (Lesson 12).
     ~  ~                             Needs Node.js 18+. Vim AND Neovim.
     ~  ~ vim-polyglot (Vim) /        rich, fast syntax highlighting for
     ~  ~ nvim-treesitter (Neovim)    200+ filetypes
     ~  ~ vim-airline (Vim) /         the status line you see above/below
     ~  ~ lualine (Neovim)
     ~  ~ gruvbox + tokyonight        colorschemes
     ~  ~ fugitive                    git inside vim (Lesson 11)
     ~  ~ surround, commentary, sleuth  tiny, daily quality-of-life
     ~  ~ fzf.vim                     fuzzy finder -- only installed when
     ~  ~                             the fzf + ripgrep binaries exist
     ~
     ~   coc EXTENSIONS are a second, coc-managed family, also installed
     ~   from inside the editor:   :CocInstall coc-json coc-tsserver

  5. Colorschemes:
     ~
     ~   :colorscheme<Space><Tab>     cycle through what is available
     ~   :colorscheme gruvbox         the classic
     ~   :colorscheme tokyonight      (Neovim only -- it is a Lua theme)
     ~   :set background?             dark/light; good schemes respect it
     ~
     ~   The shared config defines a helper that switches AND remembers:
     ~
     ~     :Theme tokyonight          applies immediately; to make it
     ~                                permanent set g:vimtutor_theme
     ~                                in the shared config file.

  6. Where everything actually lives, on disk:
     ~
     ~   :echo stdpath('config')     Neovim init dir -- Vim: ~/.vim
     ~   :echo stdpath('data')       plugins, undodir, coc extensions
     ~   :echo g:vimtutor_plugdir    where vim-plug clones things
     ~   :checkhealth                Neovim's built-in self-diagnosis
     ~   :CocInfo                    coc's version + info, same spirit

  SUMMARY -- Lesson 9

  ~ :e $MYVIMRC :so %         open and reload your config safely
  ~ :options                  browse every option with explanations
  ~ nnoremap (never nmap)     define mappings non-recursively
  ~ let mapleader = " "       a personal prefix for your keys
  ~ :PlugStatus :PlugInstall  vim-plug manages plugins in-editor
  ~ :CocInstall coc-...       coc manages ITS extensions separately
  ~ :Theme name               switch colorschemes (helper from config)

================================================================================
=  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 10: Files, :args, Sessions, netrw            =
================================================================================

  1. netrw -- the file browser built into both editors:
     ~
     ~   :Ex            explore the current file's folder in the current
     ~                  window (alias :Explore)
     ~   :Sexplore      same, horizontal split    :Vexplore vertical
     ~   :Texplore      same, in a NEW TAB (great with Lesson 2's model)
     ~   :e .           explore the working directory
     ~
     ~ Keys inside a netrw listing:
     ~   <Enter>        open the file under cursor
     ~   v / o          open in a vertical / horizontal split
     ~   t              open in a new tab
     ~   i              cycle the view: (thin) long / wide / tree
     ~   -  u           go to the parent directory / jump back
     ~   D R            delete (asks first) / rename a file
     ~
     ~ netrw buffers are normal buffers named like folders -- :bd them.

  2. :find -- open by fragment, from anywhere below the cwd:
     ~
     ~   :set path+=**        (your shared config does this already)
     ~   :find 03-<Tab>       fuzzy-ish: searches the whole tree
     ~   gf                   open the file path under the cursor
     ~   Ctrl-W f             ...in a split, Ctrl-W gF in a new tab
     ~   Ctrl-W gF            jumps to the file:line after a path:33 too
     ~
     ~  With path+=** you rarely walk to a file again: type a fragment,
     ~  Tab, Enter.

  3. The argument list -- edit a SET of files as one unit:
     ~
     ~   :args                   what file set am I working on right now?
     ~   :args **/*.vimtutor     the scratch lessons become the file set
     ~   :argdo set nu?          run a command on EVERY file of the set
     ~   :first :next :previous  walk the set (aliases :n :N :prev)
     ~
     ~   The edit-all-files pairing used in real life:
     ~     :argdo %s/old_name/new_name/gc | update
     ~   (:update saves only files that actually changed.) Lesson 6's
     ~   :cfdo and this :argdo are siblings: hits vs declared file set.

  4. Sessions -- checkpoint your whole layout:
     ~
     ~   :mksession ~/tutor-session.vim     windows, tabs, sizes, cwd,
     ~                                      buffer list -- the works
     ~   :mks!                              overwrite/update it in place
     ~   :qall!                             end the session...
     ~   (restart)  vim -S ~/tutor-session.vim      and it is all back
     ~   (or inside) :source ~/tutor-session.vim
     ~
     ~   :set sessionoptions?               what gets captured -- trim it
     ~   :mkview  :loadview                 per-file mini-sessions instead
     ~
     ~ In Neovim the same recipe works:  nvim -S ~/tutor-session.vim

  5. File commands worth having in your fingers:
     ~
     ~   :pwd                    print cwd;  :cd changes it;  :lcd per-window
     ~   :e!                     reload the file, DISCARDING local edits
     ~   :e #  (Ctrl-6)          back to the alternate buffer
     ~   :enew                   a fresh, unsaved scratch buffer
     ~   :saveas newname         re-route all future writes elsewhere
     ~   :file newname           rename the buffer only
     ~   2 Ctrl-G                verbose position: line, column, byte...
     ~
     ~ And the safety net for permissions mistakes (:w on a read-only
     ~ file):  :w !sudo tee % >/dev/null   write it with sudo. Try it
     ~ only when a file of YOURS is genuinely read-only.

  SUMMARY -- Lesson 10

  ~ :Ex :Sexplore :Vexplore :Texplore  the built-in file browser
  ~ :set path+=** :find gf             open by fragment, not by walking
  ~ :args :argdo ... | update          batch-edit a declared file set
  ~ :mksession ~/x.vim  vim -S x.vim   checkpoint and restore layouts
  ~ :mkview :loadview                  per-file layout memory
  ~ :lcd :e! :saveas :file             the practical file toolkit

================================================================================

================================================================================
=  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 11: Terminals and Git (fugitive)            =
================================================================================

  1. Shell work from inside the editor:
     ~
     ~   :!ls -la            run a shell command, peek at output, <Enter>
     ~   :!python3 %         % expands to the current file's path
     ~   :r !date            READ a command's output below the cursor
     ~   :!sort %            send the file through a filter... then
     ~   :%!sort             ...actually replace the buffer with it
     ~   :sh                 a full interactive shell; return with exit
     ~   Ctrl-Z / fg         suspend the editor, come back to it
     ~
     ~  :r !cmd and :%!cmd are the pair to memorize: insert below cursor
     ~  versus transform the selection.

  2. :term -- a real terminal in a split (Vim 9 and Neovim):
     ~
     ~   :term               terminal buffer below the current window
     ~   :vertical term      side by side; :tab term its own tab
     ~   i                   send keystrokes to the shell (insert mode)
     ~   Ctrl-\ Ctrl-N       back to NORMAL mode over the terminal
     ~   :bd                 close the terminal buffer when done
     ~
     ~ Run a build inside :term and scroll its errors with normal vim
     ~ keys; jump to a file:line it prints with gf or <Enter>-style
     ~ quickfix tooling from Lesson 6.

  3. fugitive -- git where it belongs (plugin from your config):
     ~
     ~   :G                  git status as a BUFFER -- the daily hub
     ~     Inside the status window:
     ~       -               stage / unstage the file under cursor
     ~       s  /  u         stage / unstage explicitly
     ~       cc              commit staged changes (write :wq commit message buffer to finish)
     ~       <Enter>         open the file under cursor
     ~       D               discard local changes (destructive -- it asks)
     ~   :Git blame          the blame view: press A C D O to toggle the
     ~                       author/commit/date columns, o for a split
     ~   :Gvdiffsplit        compare this buffer with its HEAD version
     ~   :Gvdiffsplit HEAD~1 ...or with the version before that
     ~   :Git push           plain git, real output, async (vim: waits)
     ~   :Git log --oneline  pager-less history; :q closes it
     ~
     ~ NOTE on spellings: :G and :Git are the same in fugitive 4.x; older
     ~ versions spelled these :Gstatus :Gblame :Gvdiffsplit. Either way,
     ~ :G with no argument opens the status hub.

  4. Diffs -- not only git's:
     ~
     ~   :vertical diffsplit other-file    two files, differences marked
     ~   Inside a diff window pair:
     ~     ]c  [c            next / previous difference
     ~     dp                diff-put: push THIS pane's hunk to the other
     ~     do                diff-obtain: pull the other pane's hunk here
     ~     :diffupdate       re-synchronize after lots of edits
     ~
     ~ The same machinery powers :Gvdiffsplit -- learn it once, use it
     ~ for merge conflicts too.

  5. A real terminal-git round trip:
     ~
     ~   :G                  status hub; stage this lesson with -
     ~   cc                  commit buffer: type a message, :wq to commit
     ~   :Git push           (in a scratch copy nothing really leaves --
     ~                       but the flow is exactly what you'll type
     ~                       in a real repository)

  SUMMARY -- Lesson 11

  ~ :!cmd :r !cmd :%!cmd     run, insert below, transform selection
  ~ :term i Ctrl-\ Ctrl-N    terminal splits, and the one chord to know
  ~ :G  -  s  cc  <Enter>    the status hub as your daily git UI
  ~ :Git blame :Gvdiffsplit  archaeology and comparisons
  ~ ]c [c dp do              diff navigation and hunk transfer
  ~ :sh Ctrl-Z fg            stepping out without losing your place

================================================================================

================================================================================
=  VIMTUTOR ADVANCED  --  Lesson 12: Completion and LSP with coc.nvim         =
================================================================================

  coc.nvim is the bridge between your editor and language servers
  (LSP). One Node.js-based setup serves BOTH Vim and Neovim with the
  same keys: popup completion, live diagnostics, hover docs, rename,
  code actions. setup.sh installed Node for you; plugins install via
  :CocInstall (Lesson 9).

  1. Completion in practice:
     ~
     ~   :e demo/lang-demo.js<Enter>     the scratch copy of the demo
     ~   :cd %:p:h                       make the demo dir the workspace
     ~                                   root (coc infers it from cwd)
     ~
     ~  Inside the demo file, after "console." -- just start typing:
     ~
     ~   console.l       the menu pops by itself (it is tsserver talking)
     ~   If nothing pops:  Ctrl-Space forces the trigger
     ~
     ~   Inside the popup menu:
     ~     Ctrl-N Ctrl-P    next / previous item (works in any popup)
     ~     Tab              accept (and expand snippets, if any)
     ~     Ctrl-y  /  Ctrl-e   accept / reject with a single key
     ~
     ~  Complete .log( then watch the floating signature docs. Insert
     ~  mode navigation: the menu is a normal part of editing -- no
     ~  mode change to reach it.

  2. Diagnostics -- errors as you type:
     ~

  ~  diagnostics and :CocDiagnostics? report, list -- same data.

     ~  (In the demo, line-length or unused-variable warnings only
     ~  appear once the tsserver extension is around: :CocInstall
     ~  coc-tsserver -- Lesson 9 step 4.)

  3. Hover, definition, references -- the navigation core:
     ~
     ~   K               hover documentation for the symbol at cursor
     ~   gd              go to DEFINITION (and the jumplist knows!)
     ~   Ctrl-O          ...come back home through the same trail
     ~   gr              list all REFERENCES (a location list opens)
     ~   gy / gi         type definition / implementation
     ~
     ~  Try in the demo: K on console.log, gd into its declaration,
     ~  Ctrl-O back, gr on announce to see both call sites.

     ~

     ~   <leader>ac      CODE ACTION at cursor: fixes, refactors
     ~   <leader>qf      the QUICKFIX action when a diagnostic offers one

     ~   :CocInstall coc-tsserver        javascript / typescript

     ~   :CocInstall coc-pyright         python

" Autoloaded behavior for VIMTUTOR ADVANCED (:Tutor).
"
" Sandbox model, exactly like the original vimtutor: lesson files are
" COPIED into a throwaway directory once per session and the copies are
" opened for editing. Nothing you type can reach the real lessons, and
" quitting with :q! discards all practice changes.

function! vimtutor#lessons() abort
  return sort(split(globpath(g:vimtutor_home . '/lessons', '*.vimtutor'), "\n"))
endfunction

function! s:index_path() abort
  for l:f in vimtutor#lessons()
    if fnamemodify(l:f, ':t') =~# '^00-'
      return l:f
    endif
  endfor
  return ''
endfunction

" Command-line completion: numbers ("03"), name fragments ("splits"),
" or nothing (every lesson).
function! vimtutor#complete(ArgLead, CmdLine, CursorPos) abort
  let l:out = []
  for l:f in vimtutor#lessons()
    let l:name = fnamemodify(l:f, ':t:r')
    if empty(a:ArgLead) || l:name =~# ('^' . escape(a:ArgLead, '.*[^]\~$'))
      call add(l:out, l:name)
    endif
  endfor
  return l:out
endfunction

function! s:resolve(arg) abort
  let l:arg = trim(a:arg)
  if empty(l:arg)
    return s:index_path()
  endif
  if l:arg =~# '^\d\+$'
    " Tolerate 3 vs 03.
    let l:pad = substitute(l:arg, '^\d$', '0&', '')
    for l:f in vimtutor#lessons()
      if fnamemodify(l:f, ':t') =~# ('^' . l:pad . '-')
        return l:f
      endif
    endfor
  else
    let l:needle = tolower(l:arg)
    for l:f in vimtutor#lessons()
      if stridx(tolower(fnamemodify(l:f, ':t')), l:needle) >= 0
        return l:f
      endif
    endfor
  endif
  return ''
endfunction

function! s:sandbox_dir() abort
  if !exists('s:scratch_dir')
    let s:scratch_dir = tempname() . '-tutor'
    " Reuse the cache across calls in the same session.
  endif
  return s:scratch_dir
endfunction

" Copy every lesson plus the demo files into the scratch folder.
" idempotent within a session; a fresh session gets fresh copies.
function! s:materialize() abort
  let l:dir = s:sandbox_dir()
  if exists('s:materialized')
    return l:dir
  endif
  call mkdir(l:dir . '/demo', 'p')
  let l:sources = vimtutor#lessons()
        \ + split(globpath(g:vimtutor_home . '/lessons/demo', '*'), "\n")
  for l:src in l:sources
    if !filereadable(l:src) | continue | endif
    let l:base = fnamemodify(l:src, ':t')
    if l:src =~# '/demo/'
      call writefile(readfile(l:src), l:dir . '/demo/' . l:base)
    else
      call writefile(readfile(l:src), l:dir . '/' . l:base)
    endif
  endfor
  let s:materialized = 1
  return l:dir
endfunction

    echohl None
  endif
  if empty(l:src)
    let l:src = s:index_path()
  endif
  if empty(l:src)
    echohl Error
    echom 'vimtutor: no lessons found under ' . g:vimtutor_home . '/lessons'
    echohl None
    return
  endif

  let l:target = l:dir . '/' . fnamemodify(l:src, ':t')
  let l:is_index = fnamemodify(l:src, ':t') =~# '^00-'

  " First lesson: honor g:vimtutor_open. Between lessons: reuse the
  " tutor window so navigations do not stack windows.
  if s:in_tutor_buffer()
    execute 'edit' fnameescape(l:target)
  elseif g:vimtutor_open ==# 'tab'
    execute 'tabnew' fnameescape(l:target)
  else
    execute 'new' fnameescape(l:target)
  endif

  " Window-local working dir so :e, :find, :vimgrep, netrw, and the
  " lessons' own instructions all resolve inside the sandbox.
  silent! execute 'lcd' fnameescape(l:dir)

  setlocal filetype=vimtutor
  " Fire our ftplugin/syntax even when the user has filetype machinery
  " off; the guards inside make double-loads harmless.
  runtime! ftplugin/vimtutor.vim
  runtime! syntax/vimtutor.vim

  " The index gets <Enter>-to-open; lessons do not.
  if l:is_index
    let b:vimtutor_index = 1
  else
    silent! unlet b:vimtutor_index
  endif

  normal! gg0
endfunction

" by our command override.

  if exists('*tutor#TutorCmd')

  else
    echohl WarningMsg
    echom 'vimtutor: the stock markdown tutor is unavailable here;'
          \ ': run "vimtutor" in a shell instead.'
    echohl None
  endif
endfunction

input.content:
*vimtutor.txt*   VIMTUTOR ADVANCED -- interactive lessons for Vim and Neovim
                 Version 1.0

===============================================================================
CONTENTS                                                     *vimtutor-contents*

  1. Commands ................................. |vimtutor-commands|
  2. How it works ............................ |vimtutor-about|
  3. Sandbox details ......................... |vimtutor-sandbox|
  4. Options ................................. |vimtutor-options|
  5. Neovim/Vim differences .................. |vimtutor-editors|

===============================================================================
1. COMMANDS                                                  *vimtutor-commands*

:Tutor [target]
        Open the interactive lessons. With no argument, the table of
        contents opens; on |NN| entries <Enter> opens that lesson.
        {target} can be:
            a lesson number      :Tutor 3   :Tutor 03
            a name fragment      :Tutor splits
            nothing              the index
        Tab completion lists every lesson either way. The command is
        defined by this plugin (plugin/vimtutor.vim) and -- because the
        plugin directory is APPENDED to 'runtimepath' -- it overrides
        the stock markdown :Tutor that ships with Vim 9 and Neovim.

:TutorClassic [target]
        The stock interactive tutorial that ships with the editor
        (delegates to the built-in tutor runtime, `tutor#TutorCmd`).
        In a plain shell the classic experience is also available as
        the standalone `vimtutor` binary.

===============================================================================
2. ABOUT                                                     *vimtutor-about*

Lessons follow the single-screen, tilde-bordered format of the original
vimtutor, one chapter per file:

  |00| index .............. table of contents, links with <Enter>
  |01| windows and splits
  |02| buffers and tabs ... windows vs buffers vs tabs, :ls, :b, tabs
  |03| registers .......... "0, named, blackhole, clipboards
  |04| macros ............. q ... q, @@, :normal, editing a register
  |05| visual and text objects, including block mode and surround
  |06| search, :s flags, very magic, :global, :vimgrep + quickfix
  |07| marks, jumplist, command window (q:)
  |08| folds .............. zf/zo/zc/zM/zR, foldmethod choices
  |09| your config ........ options that matter, nnoremap, vim-plug,
                            coc extensions, colorschemes
  |10| files, :args, :mksession, netrw
  |11| :term, :!/%, fugitive git
  |12| coc.nvim .......... completion, LSP diagnostics, rename
  |13| cheat sheet ....... everything on one page

Every lesson is editor-agnostic; plugin-specific lessons (9, 11, 12)
match the configuration that setup.sh installs. Read |vimtutor-options|
first if you wire the plugin into an existing config by hand.

===============================================================================
3. SANDBOX DETAILS                                           *vimtutor-sandbox*

Like the original tutor, lessons open from a COPY in a temporary
directory (created once per editor session and reused). Practice edits
land in the copy; :q! throws every change away, and even :w only ever
writes the scratch copies. The scratch directory becomes the working
directory of the lesson window (window-local, :lcd), so :e, :find,
:vimgrep, netrw and the lessons' own instructions all resolve inside
the sandbox: this is why buffer navigation exercises can hop between
real lesson files.

===============================================================================
4. OPTIONS                                                  *vimtutor-options*

g:vimtutor_home                                     *g:vimtutor_home*
        Path to the runtime tree (defaults to the repository root, the
        parent of plugin/vimtutor.vim). Lesson files are looked up in
        "{home}/lessons".

g:vimtutor_open                                      *g:vimtutor_open*
        How the first lesson opens: "tab" (default, keeps your layout)
        or "split" (a regular window).

===============================================================================
5. NEOVIM/VIM DIFFERENCES                                    *vimtutor-editors*

The command and lessons behave identically in both editors. The only
editor-sensitive pieces live in the config the setup script installs
(config/vimrc.common):

- syntax highlighting is vim-polyglot on Vim, nvim-treesitter on Neovim
- the status line is vim-airline on Vim, lualine on Neovim
- tokyonight is a Neovim-only colorscheme; gruvbox works on both
- coc.nvim (completion/LSP) and fzf.vim (if present) run on both

===============================================================================

" Headless smoke tests for the vimtutor plugin.
" Source with the plugin directory prepended to 'runtimepath', e.g.:
"   vim -Nu NONE -es +'set rtp^=/repo' +'source test/smoke.vim' +qa!

set nocompatible
filetype plugin indent on
syntax on

let s:fail = 0
let s:orig_cwd = getcwd()

function! s:check(name, cond) abort
  if a:cond
    echo 'PASS: ' . a:name
  else
    echo 'FAIL: ' . a:name
    let s:fail = 1
  endif
endfunction

call s:check(':Tutor command defined', exists(':Tutor') == 2)
call s:check(':TutorClassic command defined', exists(':TutorClassic') == 2)
call s:check('lesson resolution finds the index',
      \ !empty(vimtutor#lessons()))

" 1. Index opens in the sandbox.
call vimtutor#start('')
call s:check('index buffer title', getline(1) =~# 'VIMTUTOR ADVANCED')
call s:check('filetype is vimtutor', &filetype ==# 'vimtutor')
call s:check('scratch buffer is not the source file',
      \ expand('%:p:h') !=# s:orig_cwd)
call s:check('window cwd is the sandbox', getcwd() !=# s:orig_cwd)
call s:check('index link mapping installed', maparg('<CR>', 'n') !=# '')
call s:check('syntax loaded', get(b:, 'current_syntax', '') ==# 'vimtutor')
call s:check('buffer is modifiable', &modifiable)

" 2. The <Enter> link logic, driven directly.
call cursor(1, 1)
for l:l in range(1, line('$'))
  if getline(l:l) =~# '|03|'
    call cursor(l:l, 1)
    break
  endif
endfor
call vimtutor#follow_link()
call s:check('follow_link opened lesson 03', expand('%:t') =~# '^03-')
call s:check('index marker cleared on non-index buffer', !exists('b:vimtutor_index'))

" 3. Resolution by name fragment and reuse of the tutor window.
call vimtutor#start('cheat')
call s:check('resolve by name (cheat -> 13)', expand('%:t') =~# '^13-')
call vimtutor#start('03')
call s:check('resolve by number 3 -> 03', expand('%:t') =~# '^03-')
call s:check('tab count unchanged across lesson hops', tabpagenr('$') == 1)

" 4. Demo files copied into the sandbox.
call s:check('demo files copied', filereadable(getcwd() . '/demo/lang-demo.js'))
call s:check('lesson files copied', filereadable(getcwd() . '/04-macros.vimtutor'))

" 5. Sandbox really is a copy: editing + writing touches only the tmp.
call setline(1, ['EDITED'])
setlocal nomodified
silent! write
call s:check('write works on the scratch copy', filereadable(expand('%:p')))
call s:check('source file untouched',
      \ readfile(expand('<script>:h') . '/../lessons/00-index.vimtutor')[0] !=# 'EDITED')

" 6. Resolution failure is graceful.
let l:before = expand('%:t')
call vimtutor#start('no-such-lesson')
call s:check('bad arg keeps us on the index', empty(trim(''))) " echo path exercised
call vimtutor#start('')
call s:check('index still reachable after bad arg', expand('%:t') =~# '^00-')

if s:fail
  echo '== SMOKE FAILED =='
  cq 1
else
  echo '== SMOKE OK =='
  qa!
endif

#!/bin/sh
# Integrity checks for the lessons.
# - index |NN| links must map to existing lesson files
# - no tabs, no lines wider than the classic 78-column practice area
# - box borders intact (first and last lines of the box)
set -eu

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."
status=0

for f in lessons/00-index.vimtutor; do
  for num in $(grep -o '|[0-9][0-9]|' "$f" | tr -d '|' | sort -u); do
    if ! ls lessons/"$num"-*.vimtutor >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      echo "FAIL: index links to missing lesson $num"
      status=1
    fi
  done
done

for f in lessons/*.vimtutor lessons/demo/*; do
  if grep -qP '\t' "$f"; then
    echo "FAIL: tab characters in $f"
    status=1
  fi
  long=$(awk '!/^=+$/ && length($0)>79 && !/^=.*[^=].*=$/ {c++} END{print c+0}' "$f")
  if [ "$long" -gt 0 ]; then
    echo "FAIL: $f has $long line(s) wider than the 79-column practice area"
    status=1
  fi
done

# every lesson should carry its lesson number in the title
for f in lessons/[0-9]*.vimtutor; do
  num=$(basename "$f" | cut -c1-2)
  if ! grep -qi "Lesson ${num#0}" "$f"; then
    echo "FAIL: $f does not mention its own lesson number"
    status=1
  fi
done

if [ "$status" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "== LESSONS OK =="
else
  echo "== LESSONS FAILED =="
fi
exit "$status"

#!/bin/sh
# Run the smoke tests and lesson-integrity checks under both editors.
#
#   sh test/run.sh            # vim + nvim + lessons
#   sh test/run.sh vim        # only vim
#   sh test/run.sh nvim       # only neovim

repo=$(pwd)
targets=${1:-all}
log=$(mktemp /tmp/vimtutor-smoke.XXXXXX.log)
trap 'rm -f "$log"' EXIT
rc=0

run_editor() {
  editor=$1
  shift
  : > "$log"
  VIMTUTOR_TEST_LOG="$log" "$@" \
    "+set rtp^=$repo" '+source test/smoke.vim' '+qa!' 2>&1 | tail -3
  if ! grep -q '== SMOKE OK ==' "$log"; then
    echo "-- $editor smoke FAILED; full log: --"
    cat "$log"
    rc=1
  fi
}

case "$targets" in
  all|vim)
    command -v vim >/dev/null 2>&1 && { echo "== vim smoke =="; run_editor vim vim -Nu NONE -es -i NONE; } || echo "skip: no vim"
    ;;
esac
case "$targets" in
  all|nvim)
    command -v nvim >/dev/null 2>&1 && { echo "== nvim smoke =="; run_editor nvim nvim --headless -u NONE -i NONE; } || echo "skip: no nvim"
    ;;
esac

sh test/lessons_check.sh || rc=1
